item.title: Reconstructing Natural Images from Brain Activity during Natural Vision
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Tejasvi Kothapalli, Ryan Ressmeyer, Declan Rowley, Gregory D. Horwitz, Jude Mitchell, Alexander C. Huk, Bruno Olshausen, Jacob Yates
arXiv:2611.31989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing images from brain activity has two broad goals. The first is to build brain-computer interfaces. The second is to understand how the brain sees. The eyes deliver incomplete, noisy input, so the brain must fill in the gaps with its expectations of what natural scenes look like. This filling-in relies on the brain's prior over natural images. Image reconstruction lets us test which natural image prior best matches the brain's natural image prior. However, most previous work on image reconstruction relies on an unnatural condition: subjects must hold their eyes still. In reality, primates constantly move their eyes to see the world. We introduce a framework for reconstructing images from neural activity while a primate freely views a static natural scene. We record from five monkeys with high-density electrode arrays in the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and primary visual cortex (V1). The recorded receptive fields cover only a small part of the image. Thus, we combine neural activity across eye movements, trials, and sessions to reconstruct the full image. We first present a simple linear method with a 1/f prior. We then scale this approach up with modern deep learning. We train a decoder by tokenizing spiking activity and measured gaze; these tokens are fed into a transformer and diffusion model to reconstruct the full scene. Three factors determine reconstruction quality: the amount of neural evidence combined over viewing time, the accuracy of eye tracking, and the choice of image prior. Our method sets a new state-of-the-art performance in reconstructing natural images from brain activity, across brain recording modalities: fMRI, EEG, MEG and electrophysiology.

item.title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Haoyuan Li, Wei Huang, Jiehong Lin, Shengrong Zhang, Chenzhi Liu, Shengchao Zhou, Hehe Fan, Xiaojuan Qi, Yi Yang
arXiv:2611.32639v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $\pi_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $\pi_{0.5}$. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

item.title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Rafay Mohiuddin, Jiaqi Chen, Marc Pollefeys, Hermann Blum
arXiv:2611.32967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce

item.title: EgoPathBench: Evaluating Zero-Shot Egocentric Waypoint Decision-Making in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yang Zhao, Zhuo Chen, Xubo Yang
arXiv:2609.16610v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Widely used spatial-QA benchmarks increasingly motivate embodied navigation, yet evaluate foundation vision-language models (VLMs) through isolated queries about space rather than feasible action sequences in space. However, zero-shot waypoint navigation requires turning spatial understanding into a feasible action sequence: from a single first-person view, a model must jointly ground the target, respect agent-specific clearance, maintain edge-by-edge legality, and stop at the goal. To evaluate this capability, we introduce EgoPathBench, a dataset and five-task benchmark for first-person waypoint decision-making. Each example pairs an egocentric RGB image, a natural-language goal, and numbered visible waypoints, and scores predicted candidate sets or ordered routes against registered 3D scene geometry under task-specific Point or Embodied feasibility graphs. EgoPathBench comprises 31,852 training, 1,345 validation, and 1,111 benchmark questions, with at least one verified reference route for every route question. Across ten foundation VLMs, the highest EgoPath Score is only 35.6. While models often make locally plausible choices and the top model reaches 41.7% success on Point Path, it drops to 10.0% on both Embodied Path and Intent Path, with the remaining nine models below 3% on Embodied Path (and at most 4.0% on Intent Path) -- exposing a sharp gap between local plausibility and complete embodied routes. Beyond evaluation, we construct the EgoPath-SFT training set. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-4B on EgoPath-SFT raises its EgoPath Score from 3.9 to 38.9, improves closed-loop Isaac Sim execution by 20 percentage points, and transfers consistently to three external spatial benchmarks.

item.title: SofaSpace: A Benchmark for Executable Visual Spatial Reasoning in Continuous Motion and Environment Construction
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ze Rong, Kun Shi, Zhedong Zheng
arXiv:2611.32285v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A rigid body can fit at its start and goal yet collide with a wall as it moves between them. Inspired by the moving sofa problem, we introduce SofaSpace, a benchmark for visual spatial reasoning through continuous planar rigid-body transport and environment construction. SofaSpace contains 3,000 scenes organized around three challenges: geometric compatibility, nonlocal maneuver planning, and interactive and temporal coordination. Four task views ask models to plan a motion, reconstruct a layout, design an environment that meets transport requirements, or jointly generate a layout and a motion. A separate set of 534 SofaSpace-Hard tasks tests planning and judgment. A geometric verifier checks the entire body throughout each submitted motion. On static planning tasks, endpoint agreement and continuous validity differ substantially within the same submitted plans: Claude drops from 97.2% to 52.8%, DeepSeek from 100.0% to 30.6%, and Kimi from 97.2% to 29.4%, while the strongest configuration retains 98.3% full validity. Environment construction reveals a further gap. Of 295 feasible layouts generated by the strongest configuration, 181 satisfy all evaluated functional requirements; for Kimi, one of 172 does. These results show how executable checks distinguish endpoint agreement from valid motion and geometric feasibility from functional compliance.

item.title: Fast Anatomy-Aware Diffeomorphic Augmentation for Brain MRI
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Tonmoy Hossain, Alexandra G. Roberts, Mark Olchanyi, Jonathan Williams Ramirez, Stefan Brandst\"atter, Juan Eugenio Iglesias
arXiv:2611.31524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data augmentation is essential for training deep learning models that are generalizable, particularly when training data are limited. In brain MRI, augmentation methods that synthesize anatomically diverse images without relying on large cohorts are particularly attractive, especially when training supervised models for scans with a specific resolution or MRI contrast. While conventional random nonlinear fields offer a simple means of achieving such diversity, they fail to capture the underlying spatial dependencies among morphological changes across brain regions. To address this limitation, we introduce BrainAug, an anatomy-aware augmentation framework that generates diverse, anatomically coordinated deformations without relying on population imaging data. BrainAug constructs an anatomical graph encoding spatial proximity and bilateral correspondence between brain regions, then incorporates these relationships into a probabilistic model designed to sample correlated regional volume changes. These sampled variations are translated into diffeomorphic transformations, enabling substantial structural changes while preserving anatomical topology. Combined with contrast-agnostic image synthesis, BrainAug generates training images with independently varying anatomy and appearance. Evaluations across eight brain MRI datasets demonstrate stronger segmentation generalization across diverse populations, while registration experiments show improved alignment under substantial morphological differences.

item.title: PSC-Gen: Physical Sequence Conditioning for Video Generation via Agentic Visual Planning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Wonsik Shin, Jinju Jang, Junhoo Lee, Yeonjin Chang, Jimyeong Kim, Nojun Kwak
arXiv:2611.28756v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled the synthesis of high-fidelity, visually compelling videos. However, despite being trained on internet-scale video data, understanding underlying physical laws and generating physically plausible dynamics remain challenging. To mitigate this, conditioning video generators on explicit physical reasoning has emerged as a promising direction. Nevertheless, existing conditioning approaches often fail to incorporate detailed physical guidance into generation, resulting in physically implausible motion or visual artifacts. We propose PSC-Gen, a training-free framework that employs an agentic approach to synthesize visual conditions and inject their core dynamics via low-frequency filtering. By iteratively planning physical states and verifying generated keyframes, our Physics Agent constructs visually and physically consistent keyframe sequences. We then interpolate these keyframes into a continuous physical sequence and inject only its low-frequency components, steering the video model to preserve physical dynamics while synthesizing fine visual details. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that PSC-Gen faithfully follows instructions and generates physically plausible videos.

item.title: Biomechanically Grounded Prediction of Selective Motor Control and Clinical Outcomes from Infant Video
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Divya Joshi, Ruize Yang, Colleen Peyton, R. James Cotton
arXiv:2611.32890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Early identification of cerebral palsy (CP) relies on observational assessments of spontaneous infant movement, such as the General Movement Assessment (GMA) and the Baby Observational Selective Control AppRaisal (BabyOSCAR), which require trained raters and substantial scoring time. Existing automated approaches derive hand-engineered features from two-dimensional keypoints, which describe image-plane motion rather than the three-dimensional behavior of individual joints. We present Baby Biomechanical 3D Body (BB3D), an infant-adapted, biomechanical pipeline that estimates joint-angle trajectories from single-camera video. Against a multi-view markerless motion capture reference in 17 infants, BB3D's median Procrustes-aligned error was 17.5~mm for joint centers and 20.4~mm for marker sites. A spatio-temporal transformer, pretrained on BB3D joint-angle trajectories from 1k+ single-camera recordings, and fine-tuned on 550 videos from 350 infants, predicted each individual BabyOSCAR item with a mean within-site AUC of 0.79 and the BabyOSCAR total with a Spearman correlation of 0.86 on held-out recordings. Without being trained on diagnosis, the predicted total separated infants with CP from those without CP with an AUC of 0.86, exceeding a replicated two-dimensional feature classifier (0.67) but below the expert clinician rater's total (0.97). Predicted scores also carried information about functional ability and body distribution, though less than expert clinician scores. These results show that biomechanically grounded representations of monocular video can support scalable, joint-level assessment of selective motor control in infancy

item.title: StreamCoach: Proactive Sports Coaching via Continuous Visual Reasoning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xiaoye Liang, Yiming Huang, Jialu Wu, Yushe Cao, Ruxiang Duan, Yi Sun, Tie Liu, Lai Jiang, Mai Xu, Shikun Feng, Yiheng Zhu
arXiv:2611.32281v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In fitness and sports training, timely action quality assessment (AQA) is essential for learners to identify and correct technical errors during movement execution. However, most AQA methods assess completed performances, limiting their ability to provide timely feedback. Streaming methods alleviate this latency, but limited reasoning hinders their use of subtle movement cues and sport-specific knowledge. Moreover, their fragmented feedback focuses on one body part at a time, overlooking movement details of other body parts and transitions between action phases. To address these limitations, we propose StreamCoach, a streaming AQA framework under the OnCueCoaching paradigm that couples continuous chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning with proactive, evidence-gated coaching. Technique-Aware Reasoning tracks body-part movements and action-phase transitions against sport-specific criteria, while Holistic Coaching integrates accumulated evidence to deliver timely, comprehensive feedback on strengths and technical errors. To support training and benchmarking, we construct EE4D-Stream from 1,213 sports video sequences in Ego-Exo4D through LLM-assisted reannotation and manual review of selected claims, pairing dense CoT annotations with evidence-gated speech content. Building on this dataset, we train StreamCoach using Temporal-Semantic Alignment Reinforcement Learning to jointly optimize feedback timing and content. We benchmark 11 offline and streaming baselines on EE4D-Stream, including three proprietary models. StreamCoach achieves state-of-the-art results across intervention timing, action assessment, and coaching quality, surpassing both GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5.

item.title: Clinical3D-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Spatial Intelligence of Multimodal LLMs in Hospital Environments
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yang Bai, Yingzhi Xia, Ling Lin, Jun Cheng, Lin Fu, Huazhu Fu
arXiv:2611.32094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Spatial reasoning in hospitals requires tracking look-alike equipment, interpreting patient-relative directions, and judging passage widths, yet existing benchmarks provide limited coverage of these abilities. We introduce Clinical3D-Bench, a simulated benchmark with 3,368 questions of eight types on egocentric walkthroughs of 373 hospital-room layouts. Layouts follow hospital design guidelines, answers are computed from the 3D scenes, and paired scene states test whether models change their answers when relevant evidence changes. Videos are photorealistic, and ten physicians screened the layouts. Among 35 multimodal large language models (MLLMs), the best open and proprietary models reach 45.7% and 53.6% macro accuracy, against 40.8% for an answer prior and 79.0% for physicians on a subset, and 27 of 32 open models score below 40% on two-way patient-relative directions. Fine-tuning on Clinical3D-45K, our 44,750-question training set, lifts two MLLMs 16-20 points above the best proprietary model. 3D maps given to the fine-tuned MLLM as input go largely unused: replacing them with another video's, even when they are ground truth, barely changes its accuracy. The proposed GeoJeV instead lets the MLLM compute with 3D: it reconstructs a scene memory from each video, selects 3D operations and their arguments from the MLLM's question state, and adds their evidence to its option scores. It achieves the highest accuracy of all evaluated models, narrowing the gap to physicians.

item.title: Beyond Expert Replay: Cross-Instruction Anchoring for Continual Vision-Language-Action Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Ziyang Chen, Dehua Chen, Shaoguang Wang, Xu Yan, Hao Huang, Tao Chen
arXiv:2611.31903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models need to continually acquire new manipulation skills while retaining the ability to follow previously learned instructions. Experience replay (ER) can mitigate catastrophic forgetting, but retaining only a small number of historical expert frames per task leaves many old-instruction responses without direct supervision. Under limited replay, we observe a structured failure mode in which an earlier instruction can trigger a subsequently learned, competing goal. To address this gap, we propose Cross-Instruction Anchoring (XIA), which supplements expert replay with instruction-conditioned response preservation. At each task boundary, XIA freezes the previous policy as a teacher and matches its responses to old instructions paired with current observations. This extends supervision beyond stored historical examples without requiring additional expert replay data. Experiments across multiple VLA architectures and three LIBERO suites demonstrate improved success rates and reduced forgetting compared with ER under identical historical expert-data budgets. Additional RoboCasa and real-world experiments further support the effectiveness of XIA.

item.title: DistMoE: Private-data Rehearsal-free Routing in Mixture-of-Experts for Distributed Instruction Tuning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Mainak Singha, Niccol\`o Biondi, Elisa Ricci, Subhankar Roy
arXiv:2608.09907v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have shown strong multimodal instruction-following ability, but adapting them to diverse visual-language domains typically assumes centralized data access and costly joint training. This is restrictive when data is distributed across private, domain-specific, or permission-limited clients. To this end, we propose DistMoE, a mixture-of-experts (MoE) approach for distributed visual instruction tuning. In each layer of the language decoder it augments the public feedforward network (FFN) with a client-specific private FFN expert, with the goal to acquire domain-specific knowledge. However, independent expert training causes the private FFNs to learn representation of different scales and magnitudes, making merging the experts difficult. To reduce client-specific drift, we introduce a public-anchored expert composition stage that updates only routers and lightweight private projection adapters on a mix of local client data and public data, via an isotropic regularization loss, therefore making it cross-client rehearsal-free composition. During inference, DistMoE performs modular routing over public and private experts, enabling token-wise domain composition without explicit domain labels. Experiments across diverse visual-language benchmarks show that DistMoE enables flexible expert reuse, effective domain adaptation, and competitive performance while preserving modular control over client-specific knowledge.

item.title: Designer-RSI: Evolving Procedural Memory from User Traffic for Graphic Design Agent
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Hongyang Du, Lan Yan, Christian Flores, Asim Kadav
arXiv:2609.22086v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Deployed software agents face a continuous stream of user requests while their foundation-model weights remain frozen between releases. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) via external memory offers a practical path to continual adaptation, yet prior methods largely assume programmatic verifiers, cheap retries, or a single global prompt. Creative software breaks these assumptions, as open-ended visual briefs lack ground truth, VLM judges are noisy, and multi-step tool executions are costly and confounded by external assets. We present Designer-RSI, which evolves a modular skill bank from unlabeled design trajectories for an agent spanning over 230 raster, vector, and layout tools. Designer-RSI couples widening (acquiring new skills for recurring capability gaps) with deepening (revising failing skills by contrasting successful and failed runs), and screens updates through a Pareto-style matched replay gate that requires strict gains on sampled briefs without local regressions. Across held-out product briefs, eight external benchmarks, and two backbones, traffic-driven evolution outperforms static documentation skills, lifts execution success up to 99.8%, improves requirement fulfillment, and reaches up to a 67.6% blind win rate over the base agent. Ablations further show that skill acquisition and revision are strongly synergistic: neither suffices alone, and reliable gains require evolving coverage and execution quality together.

item.title: See the Answer, Learn to Embed: Learning Universal Multimodal Embeddings from Hindsight
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yoonki Cho, Youngju Na, Taegeun Yang, Jinhwan Seo, Sung-Eui Yoon
arXiv:2611.32439v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Universal Multimodal Embedding (UME) models map heterogeneous multimodal inputs into a shared embedding space, where pairwise similarity supports diverse downstream tasks. Recent reasoning-driven UME approaches use intermediate reasoning to generate additional context for embedding, but often incur extra computation at inference. In this paper, we explore the matched candidate (i.e., the paired target) as an alternative source of context, asking whether a model can "see the answer" during training and "learn to embed" without it at inference. However, direct conditioning on this privileged context can introduce candidate-specific information unavailable from the query alone or cause the candidate-conditioned query representation to collapse toward the candidate embedding. To address this, we introduce Hindsight-Enhanced Multimodal Embeddings (HEME), which learns query-grounded hindsight representations from such candidate context. HEME first trains a hindsight teacher with a hindsight attention mask, mismatched-candidate conditioning, and query-token alignment to limit excessive reliance on the candidate. It then freezes the teacher and distills its hindsight representation and similarity distribution into a standalone student embedder. At inference, the student independently encodes queries and candidates without candidate conditioning or the hindsight teacher. Experiments on MMEB-V2 and the agent and text tasks of MMEB-V3 demonstrate the effectiveness of HEME and show that it enables more efficient inference than explicit reasoning-driven methods.

item.title: Physicl Scenes: An Artist-created 3D Dataset for Learning Perception and Action
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yueh-Cheng Liu, Snehal Jauhri, Matthias Nie{\ss}ner, Angela Dai
arXiv:2611.33137v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Physicl Scenes, a high-quality artist-created and curated dataset of 6,499 3D scenes spanning household rooms, public interiors, and outdoor spaces. The dataset combines detailed geometry, physically based materials, and carefully composed environments with object- and part-level semantic annotations, providing rich, joint supervision for visual and embodied learning. We demonstrate its value as training data across inverse rendering, 3D reconstruction, scene understanding, and mobile manipulation. Across these tasks, training state-of-the-art methods with our scenes improves performance over alternative synthetic datasets. In addition, we introduce a mobile manipulation benchmark, evaluating vision-language-action models performing physical pick and place in diverse 3D scenes with realistic layouts, and using our part annotations to also score where each object is grasped. Our dataset will be released publicly to facilitate research in visual and embodied AI.

item.title: From Clinical Intent to Clinical Model: Autonomous Coding-Agents for Clinician-driven AI Development
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Zihao Zhao, Eneko Cornejo Merodio, Wenya Zhao, Frederik Hauke, Wensa Peng, Xixi Song, Maike Bode, Juliana de Castilhos, Mathis Bode, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Sven Nebelung, Daniel Truhn
arXiv:2604.17110v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: BACKGROUND: Developing clinically useful AI requires collaboration between clinicians and AI developers, yet this process often involves time-consuming communication and potential misalignment. Coding agents may help bridge this gap. METHODS: We present a prototype that lets clinicians drive AI development directly via natural-language interactions. The system turns a clinician request into an executable workflow through semantic parsing, task initialization, and iterative code tuning, using Claude Opus 4.6 as the underlying coding agent. We evaluated this prototype across 12 tasks, including straightforward requests focused solely on model performance metrics and more complex requests. The test set was held out from the beginning and was never exposed to the coding agent. An exploratory human evaluation was conducted with six clinicians who completed a questionnaire rated on a five-point Likert scale after interacting with the system. RESULTS: Across 12 tasks, the prototype autonomously developed AI models with competitive performance. Notably, clinicians' practical knowledge helped reduce shortcut reliance (partial correlation from 0.53 to 0.07) in pneumothorax classification. Drain-free AUROC improved in every cohort and the clinician-driven model achieved stronger lesion localization than medical foundation models across all five external cohorts. All six participants commented communication as efficient and agreed that the agent understood their clinical goals and can provide useful suggestions, but also saying extensive external testing is needed before clinical use of autonomously developed AI models. CONCLUSIONS: These findings suggest that coding agents could let clinicians take a more independent and active role in clinical AI development, reducing their reliance on AI developers, although further improvements are needed.

item.title: TaskVICL: Task-Conditioned Decoder States for Visual In-Context Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Chenyang Wang, Jiamo Hu, Chengrui Wu, Lingyue Chen, Jianguo Chen, Xun Xu, Xulei Yang
arXiv:2611.28081v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. Common retrievers rank examples by image similarity and ignore the task, while task-aware alternatives require answer generation, external encoders or retriever training. We ask whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before it answers, can select demonstrations directly. TaskVICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature: the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, TaskVICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw achieves the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers, exceeding the strongest baseline by 3.30 points on Qwen3-VL and 1.41 on InternVL3.5, with gains carrying over to Gemma-3-12B. When the same NICO++ image is asked about its object or its context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations. A lightweight shared projection, TaskVICL-Proj, adds further gains on classification. Controls show that task text at extraction drives most of the gains, and attention analysis describes how it shifts attention toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for task-aware demonstration retrieval.

item.title: ReCoCo: From Patches to Compositions for Visual Representation Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Juan Guti\'errez, Saman Zadtootaghaj, Jos\'e Luis Blanco-Murillo, Sara Atito
arXiv:2611.24806v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Self-supervised learning has produced powerful visual representations, yet learning strong dense features remains challenging. While consistency between augmented views provides strong image-level supervision, extending this principle to local visual content is less straightforward. Existing approaches often match individual patches across views or identify coherent regions, introducing uncertainties in correspondence estimation and assumptions about how visual content should be grouped. We introduce ReCoCo (Regional Composition Consistency), a principled approach that extends cross-view consistency to the regional level without requiring such correspondences or semantic grouping. ReCoCo represents the content shared between augmented views through compositions of their patch-level predictions over learned visual prototypes. By aligning these compositions, the model learns from regions containing multiple visual concepts without requiring them to be separated beforehand. ReCoCo integrates naturally with teacher-student self-distillation and introduces no additional learned parameters. Extensive experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in frozen-feature segmentation, clustering, and regional retrieval while maintaining competitive image-level recognition, alleviating the trade-off between dense and global representation quality.

Jiangtian LiBlair C. ArmstrongYang Xuahttps://ror.org/0524sp257Department of Philosophy, University of Bristol, Bristol BS6 6JL, United Kingdombhttps://ror.org/05k33q843Department of Psychology, University of Toronto Scarborough, Toronto, ON M1C 1A4, Canadachttps://ror.org/01a28zg77Basque Center on Cognition, Brain, and Language, Donostia San Sebastián, Gipuzkoa 20009, Spaindhttps://ror.org/03dbr7087Department of Computer Science, Cognitive Science Program, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3H5, Canada

item.title: RFW-A: Agentic Procedural Generation of 400K Articulated Assets over 500 Categories
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yuanbo Lyu, Changjian Pan, Saining Zhang, Yi Yang, Peishuo Li, Zhiheng Li, Jialu Liu, Junhao Chen, Jiawei Weng, Yupeng Gao, Weiqing Xiao, Wenyi Li, Jiarui Guo, Rui Zhang, Jingrun Du, Weiyi Lin, Zenan Meng, Hu Wei, Lin Qu, Zongzheng Zhang, Hao Zhao, Chaojian Li
arXiv:2610.40333v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: High-quality articulated assets are essential for embodied perception, simulation, and manipulation, yet constructing them at scale remains difficult. Manual annotation and procedural modeling require substantial human effort. Recent agentic systems automate asset construction through program synthesis, but repeat costly reasoning and refinement for every new asset. Our key observation is that assets within a category can share construction logic despite variations in structure and appearance. Agentic synthesis and procedural generation are therefore complementary: agents can construct reusable programs, while procedural execution reuses the resulting logic across many samples. We therefore present RFW-A, which combines the two in a new articulated-asset generation paradigm. Starting from existing articulated programs, RFW-A organizes reusable components and their dependencies into category-level generators. Agents test and refine these generators across sampled configurations and motion states. Once constructed and validated, the generators produce diverse assets through procedural execution with no further model calls or token charges. The estimated API cost of generator authoring averages $10.62, amortizing to $0.05 per asset over 200 assets, versus $1.24 for the sampled per-asset agentic synthesis baseline. Using RFW-A, we built RFW-A-400K, containing over 400K sim-ready articulated assets across more than 500 categories. Experiments show high structural and kinematic validity and stable execution across physics simulators. Beyond asset validity, training with RFW-A-400K improves part-level articulation estimation on seen and unseen categories, while policies trained in simulation with retrieved and program-edited assets transfer zero-shot to real articulated objects.

item.title: CaveBench: Benchmarking Abductive Physical Reasoning from Internal Observations
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Guanxin Lin (Tsinghua University), Chen Yang (Tsinghua University), Shenxiang Zeng (Tsinghua University), Honghui Zhu (Tsinghua University), Xin Li (Tsinghua University), Wenbo Deng (Tsinghua University), Jiansheng Fan (Tsinghua University), Chen Wang (Tsinghua University)
arXiv:2611.32251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are advancing in physical reasoning, but whether they can understand external physical drivers from internal observations remains an open question. Existing benchmarks have not specifically targeted this setting. To this end, we introduce CaveBench, a benchmark for abductive physical reasoning from internal observations. Models receive apparatus descriptions and internal images while the external controls remain hidden, and must infer the operations responsible for the observed responses. CaveBench spans 20 apparatus scenes in five physical domains and contains 10,200 simulated episodes, split into 9,000 training, 1,000 validation, and 200 test episodes. Questions span one to six events and require the complete control set at every event, testing whether an explanation accounts for the entire process. Synchronized observations and control records provide the inputs and reference answers. Evaluating 27 VLM configurations yields six-event exact-match accuracies of 68.0% for the strongest closed-source model and 12.5% for the strongest open-weight model. Seven adaptation baselines show that single-event gains need not improve complete sequences. Error analysis identifies failures in visual identification, physical inference, evidence integration, and action composition, specifying where current models struggle to connect internal phenomena with their external causes.

item.title: Hi3R-VLA: Grounding Semantics and Actions in 3D
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shizhe Chen, Paul Pacaud, Cordelia Schmid
arXiv:2611.31535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While recent vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate 3D geometry, how to effectively exploit it for precise and generalizable action prediction remains a central challenge. We introduce Hi3R-VLA, a 3D policy that grounds heterogeneous modalities - vision, language, and action - in explicit 3D geometry for robotic manipulation. Our model integrates spatially-aligned visual features and language conditioning into point cloud representations, enriching scene geometry with fine-grained, task-relevant semantics. It then anchors low-level control commands in the same 3D coordinate frame and uses 3D-RoPE enhanced action-to-point attention over coarse-to-fine point features to model geometric relationships between action targets and observed points. Our analysis demonstrates the importance of semantic fusion within 3D and spatial alignment between observations and actions. With fewer than 250M trainable parameters, Hi3R-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa, RLBench, RoboTwin2, DexJoCo and DexSuite across diverse manipulation tasks and embodiments, from single-arm and dual-arm grippers to dexterous hands. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate its effectiveness in the physical world. The model, code and dataset are publicly released at https://cshizhe.github.io/projects/hi3r_vla.html.

item.title: Open-OmniCoach: Evidence-Enhanced Trajectory Learning for Omni Video Agents
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Weisong Liu, Xiangtai Li, Haochen Wang, Haiquan Wen, Zhaoxiang Zhang
arXiv:2611.31891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training capable omni video agents requires more than diverse question-answer pairs: agents must learn to reliably find, connect, and correct task-relevant evidence in omni-setting. However, we argue that existing data pipelines provide limited control over task-relevant evidence and weak supervision for these capabilities. In this work, we present Open OmniCoach, a new framework for evidence-seeking omni video agents. It contains a high-quality dataset, OmniCoach-240K, and a new agentic reinforcement learning (RL) method, Step-Level Evidence-Guided Policy Optimization (SEPO). For the former, OmniCoach-240K comprises 248.2K interaction trajectories, including 230.7K multi-span trajectories and 17.4K reflection trajectories. We design a three-stage data pipeline by leveraging both fine-grained omni-evidence and the agent's own errors. Meanwhile, compared with other RL baselines, SEPO provides turn-level credit based on improvements in evidence coverage and temporal localization. Applying both trajectory data and the SEPO method, we obtain Open OmniAgent models. The resulting models outperform the baselines across multiple video and audio-visual understanding tasks by significant margins, demonstrating the effectiveness of the Open OmniCoach framework. In particular, Open OmniAgent-30B improves average accuracy over Qwen3-Omni by 6.3 percentage points across nine benchmarks, with gains of 12.2 and 13.3 points on LVOmniBench and LVBench, respectively.

item.title: Motion Conditioned World Modeling for Embodied Visual Tracking
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Jiahao Zhang, Xuan Yao, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
arXiv:2611.32900v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models support embodied decision-making by predicting future environment states. In embodied visual tracking, uncertain target motion and robot-induced viewpoint changes jointly affect visual observations, making future-state prediction challenging. We propose Motion-Conditioned World Modeling, which incorporates predicted target-motion distributions and robot ego-motion into latent state transitions. A Geometry--Progress module jointly models geometric paths and single-step travel distances through shared motion modes and path-conditioned progress distributions. This formulation captures uncertainty in route selection and motion progress while preserving their dependence. Action-induced coordinate transformations express predicted paths in the next robot frame, providing geometrically grounded conditions for future visual-state prediction. Future visual feature reconstruction supervises the motion predictor through the conditioned transition branch, linking explicit motion representations to subsequent observations. The model is jointly optimized with motion likelihood, feature reconstruction, and expert-action supervision, enabling the tracking policy to combine visual context with predictive motion cues.Experiments on three embodied tracking benchmarks demonstrate improved tracking performance and cross-environment generalization with a lightweight $0.5$B backbone.

item.title: OVOK: A Recursive Self-Improving Agentic Framework for Video-Based Articulated Robot State Estimation
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Cheng Dai, Renkai Luo, Guanfeng Tang, Siming Li, Hao Zhao
arXiv:2611.32185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recovering articulated robot state from video supports metric spatial sensing for manipulation, scene reconstruction, and action planning. Yet the problem is ill-posed: different intrinsics, camera-to-robot poses, and joint angles can explain similar observations. Prior task-specific regressors typically assume known intrinsics, fit one robot through laborious data collection and robot-specific training, and still transfer poorly across scenes. Foundation models apply to any robot zero-shot, but their estimates have large errors. We present OVOK (One Video to Kinetics), a recursive self-improving agentic framework for this task. Under a human-authored protocol, an agentic initializer constructs robot-specific OVOK-4k; a proposer--executor--verifier loop then jointly evolves tools and executable workflows from feedback. Updated tools and workflows are accepted only when the verifier judges a positive improvement. The retained workflow is frozen for accurate inference. Experiments demonstrate that the evolved workflow achieves state-of-the-art results on DREAM-V and RoboKeyGen-V, delivering robust and accurate estimates.

item.title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yu Chen, Haosen Yang, Su Ee Tan, Zhensong Zhang, Jifei Song, Jiankang Deng
arXiv:2611.32816v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.

item.title: OmniHarness-RSI: Modality-Aware Harness Evolution for Omnimodal Understanding
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Shilin Ma, Xingming Shui, Jinglin Chen, Zetong Zhao, Jingqi Tian, Deyi Zhu, Yansong Tang
arXiv:2611.32951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in harness-based recursive self-improvement (RSI) have improved video understanding by evolving executable agent workflows without updating foundation model parameters. However, extending this paradigm to omnimodal understanding remains challenging, as the heterogeneous and interdependent nature of multimodal perception and reasoning creates a complex evolution space, making targeted harness optimization difficult. To address these challenges, we propose OmniHarness-RSI, a modality-aware framework for evolving agent harnesses. Specifically, we factorize the evolution space into three capability dimensions: modality routing and collaboration, modality-aware evidence localization, and modality-specific perception. Based on this factorization, we construct a Factorized-Harness Agent integrating specialized perception experts and audio-video retrieval tools. We further introduce modality-guided harness evolution, which identifies deficiencies through structured modality-capability attribution and refines corresponding harness strategies through interactive code revisions and execution feedback. Validation-guided selection and held-out evaluation assess generalization within and across datasets. Experiments on WorldSense, Daily-Omni, and OmniVideoBench demonstrate test accuracy improvements of 8.86, 8.13, and 6.23 percentage points, respectively, consistently outperforming modality-agnostic RSI. The evolved harnesses also demonstrate cross-dataset transfer without adaptation, while reducing planner calls and viewed frames.

item.title: Image Diffusion Models Are Good 3D Human Motion Generators
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Siyuan Yang, Chong Wang, Hao Cheng, Jun Liu, Bihan Wen, Alex Kot, Hedvig Kjellstrom
arXiv:2610.14254v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Text-to-motion generation typically relies on dataset-specific skeletal representations, with models trained separately for benchmarks with different joint layouts. We investigate whether image diffusion architectures can model 3D human motion through a common image-compatible representation that accommodates heterogeneous skeletal layouts while preserving motion-specific kinematic structure. To this end, we organize root-centered joint trajectories into topology-informed joint--time images and model global root dynamics through a complementary latent stream. A motion autoencoder conditions local-motion decoding on the root latent, while a text-conditioned Scalable Interpolant Transformer (SiT) jointly generates both latent streams, with supervision on decoded 3D joint positions further constraining generation in motion space. In addition to dataset-specific models, we train a single motion autoencoder on HumanML3D and KIT-ML, followed by a single text-conditioned SiT shared across both datasets, preserving their respective skeletal definitions without skeleton retargeting to a common joint layout. Experiments on HumanML3D and KIT-ML show that our dataset-specific models achieve state-of-the-art performance, while shared training yields further gains on both benchmarks, demonstrating the benefits of shared modeling across heterogeneous skeletal layouts.

item.title: Concepts in Motion: Temporal Concept Bottleneck Model for Interpretable Video Classification
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Patrick Knab, Sascha Marton, Philipp J. Schubert, Drago Guggiana, Christian Bartelt
arXiv:2509.20899v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) enable interpretable image classification by structuring predictions around human-understandable concepts, but extending this paradigm to video remains challenging due to the difficulty of extracting concepts and modeling them over time. In this paper, we introduce MoTIF (Moving Temporal Interpretable Framework), a transformer-based concept architecture that operates on sequences of temporally grounded concept activations, by employing per-concept temporal self-attention to model when individual concepts recur and how their temporal patterns contribute to predictions. Central to the framework is a class-conditioned VLM-based concept discovery module that extracts object- and action-centric textual concepts from training videos, yielding temporally expressive concept sets without manual concept annotation. Across multiple video benchmarks, this combination improves over global concept bottlenecks and remains competitive within the interpretable concept-bottleneck setting, while narrowing the gap to strong black-box video baselines that we report as contextual references. Code available at github.com/patrick-knab/MoTIF.

item.title: Multimodal Masked Diffusion Autoencoder for Modeling Impaired Driving
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Kayli Battel, Todd J Rowell, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Laporsha Dees, Emily Sumner, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
arXiv:2611.23211v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human cognitive state (e.g., distraction, stress), gaze, and behavior interact with the driving environment in subtle ways that AI could use to assist drivers, but ground-truth labels for human cognitive state levels are costly to obtain at scale. We propose a multimodal masked-diffusion autoencoder, ID-MAE, that adds a self-supervised objective to impairment prediction: alongside predicting the impairment label as a masked token, it reconstructs masked gaze and trajectory. To probe the effects of different modalities and types of impairments on model inference, we introduce DIVERT, a driving-simulator dataset containing 103 hours of driving data (n = 109) with ten impairment inductions spanning cognitive, visual, and emotional states, recorded with gaze, vehicle state, and scene video. We demonstrate how ID-MAE affords significant improvements in impairment inference results on both the DIVERT dataset and existing datasets, and enables strong results in additional tasks, such as trajectory and gaze prediction. For location-matched pairs, our model achieves a paired AUC of 0.706 for impairment detection on DIVERT, compared to 0.590 without reconstruction loss, improving over existing baselines. We probe the design space in terms of input modalities, masking scheme, positional encoding, attention mechanism, and decoding. We also investigate the interaction between various impairments in training and inference, demonstrating that visually demanding distractions are separable from cognitive distractions. We plan to publicly release the code and data.

item.title: HGeo-TopoMap: Boosting Topological Mapping with Hierarchical Geometric Priors
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Siyu Li, Kunyu Peng, Di Wen, Beiping Hou, Zhiyong Li, Kailun Yang
arXiv:2607.21281v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Topological maps provide essential road structure and connectivity information for autonomous driving. However, accurate centerline modeling remains challenging due to the lack of explicit visual markings and the insufficient exploitation of geometric regularities in existing methods. To address these challenges, we propose HGeo-TopoMap, a hierarchical geometric prior learning framework that integrates road-structure guidance and geometric consistency into centerline instance decoding. Specifically, a Geometric Adaptive Learning (GAL) module introduces spatially adaptive cross-attention to incorporate road structure priors derived from inverse perspective mapping, where distance-aware attention biases guide instance queries toward spatially relevant structural information. Furthermore, we develop a hierarchical centerline decoding strategy that progressively predicts instance centers and their constituent points, facilitating the learning of geometric orientations and spatial configurations. Building upon this structured representation, a Geometric Consistency Learning (GCL) module imposes layer-wise contrastive supervision on matched instance queries using geometric groupings, exploiting geometric relationships among centerline instances to regularize instance representations and improve centerline detection. By jointly exploiting spatial structural guidance and instance-level geometric regularities, HGeo-TopoMap enhances centerline detection and topology reasoning. Extensive experiments on the OpenLane-V2 centerline and lane segment benchmarks demonstrate improved topological mapping accuracy. Meanwhile, the proposed method demonstrates stable performance under the robustness benchmark. The source code and model weights will be made publicly available at https://github.com/lynn-yu/HGeo-TopoMap.

item.title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Chen Chen, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr \v{S}vec, David J. Yoon, Matthias M\"uller, Vladlen Koltun
arXiv:2611.09892v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2% and 42.9% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation. See https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-amp/ for code and videos.

item.title: TANGO: Training-free Controllable Human Motion Generation with Progressive Token Guidance
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Nhat Le, Daochang Liu, Baoru Huang, Anh Nguyen, Ajmal Mian
arXiv:2605.14935v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present TANGO, a progressive token guidance framework for training-free controllable human motion generation. Unlike control approaches that primarily operate at a fixed temporal resolution, TANGO leverages a multi-scale hierarchy of discrete motion tokens to establish a structured control process, progressively guiding global motion structure before refining local details. At each scale, the differentiable control objective guides all current-scale token distributions, and the sampled tokens condition subsequent finer-scale predictions. To address the challenge of discrete categorical sampling, we adopt a first-order approach following the Bayesian principle, adjusting token sampling distributions with a single first-order update per scale. To further improve guidance consistency, we introduce Within-Scale Interdependency (WSI) guidance to account for how token choices jointly affect the control objective, and Cross-Scale Consistency (CSC) guidance to estimate how remaining finer scales may affect the final control outcome. Together, these complementary guidance mechanisms enable consistent and effective progressive control without additional control-specific training. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of TANGO across different control objectives in terms of motion quality, control accuracy, and generalization to unseen constraints.

item.title: MemAnchorWorld: A Sparse World Model with Horizon-Conditioned Memory Retrieval for Autonomous Driving
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Xinyang Jia, Yuqi Zhang, Jiakai Wang, Yahu Yang, Guandong Pan, Chao Tong, Xianglong Liu
arXiv:2611.32745v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse world models for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting represent scenes with a small set of evolving queries to efficiently predict future geometry and semantics for autonomous driving. However, existing sparse world models face a bottleneck in using historical temporal evidence for long-horizon forecasting. They rely on scene states to carry historical information implicitly, allowing errors to propagate and accumulate across successive forecasting steps and causing geometric and semantic deviations. To address this limitation, we present MemAnchorWorld, a sparse occupancy world model that explicitly retrieves relevant historical geometric and semantic evidence for 4D semantic occupancy forecasting. Inspired by the von Restorff effect, we introduce a forecast-time-conditioned hierarchical dual-path memory-anchor retrieval mechanism. Guided by the effective age and semantic compatibility of historical information, it combines query-level candidate selection with point-level memory-anchor retrieval to provide historical evidence for sparse points at different forecast times. To better use memory anchors and existing features, a point-level residual adapter jointly gated by the task and forecast time separately controls residual corrections to semantics, occupancy confidence, and spatial positions. On Occ3D-nuScenes, MemAnchorWorld achieves an average mIoU of 13.55% and an average IoU of 22.84% across the 1-3 s forecasting horizons, attaining state-of-the-art performance on both metrics.Project page: https://memanchorworld.github.io/

item.title: Urbex: Agentic Spatial Grounding for City-Scale 3D Scenes
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Yu Wang, Rui Dai, Wei Chen, Yi Wang, Bo Dang, Kaikui Liu, Xiangxiang Chu, Yansheng Li
arXiv:2610.18356v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: City-scale 3D grounding is commonly formulated as candidate ranking, which requires precomputed instance proposals and becomes inefficient in large outdoor scenes. We propose Urbex, an agentic vision-language framework that instead casts grounding as active spatial search. Urbex represents a city-scale 3D scene as an interactive multi-view environment, allowing a VLM agent to query landmarks, zoom into local regions, render oblique views, and commit a grounded bounding box. We optimize this tool-use policy with reinforcement learning on CityRefer, using smooth localization rewards and lightweight shaping rewards for efficient exploration. Experiments show that Urbex achieves the best Hit@1 and IoU on CityRefer, supports candidate-free grounding without ground-truth boxes, and is substantially faster than the strongest city-scale ranking baseline. Zero-shot results on STPLS3D-Refer further indicate improved cross-scene robustness.

item.title: Intervenable Concept Dynamics for Video Activity Forecasting
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Patrick Knab, David Steinmann, Giovanni De Felice, Felix Divo, Udo Schlegel, Wolfgang Stammer, Sascha Marton, Christian Bartelt
arXiv:2611.00020v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Concept bottleneck models route predictions through human-understandable concepts, making their intermediate states inspectable and editable. Extending this model family to forecasting requires modeling how concept activations evolve over time as objects, actions, and their interactions change, yet existing CBMs ground concepts only in observed inputs and do not forecast their future evolution. We study this problem using videos of ongoing activities and forecast future activities through a named-concept state. We propose TRACE-CBM (Temporal Relational Activity Concept Evolution), which first refines observed concept activations with sparse spatio-temporal graphs. It then recursively predicts future concept states, conditioning each transition on the prior activity distribution, and decodes both observed and predicted states with a shared activity classifier. At inference time, the model supports editing concept values, activity activations, and learned edges without parameter updates, exposing the relational spatio-temporal dependencies used for forecasting. Across multiple datasets, TRACE improves observed-activity accuracy over concept-based methods and stays close to matched black-box forecasters in forecast accuracy. Intervention experiments show that concept edits correct part of the initially incorrect forecasts without flipping initially correct ones, and that activity-belief edits can steer forecasts toward a requested activity. Code: https://github.com/patrick-knab/TRACE-CBM

item.title: SetCon: Setup-Conditioned IMU-Language Learning from 3D Human Motion
item.description:
Relevance: 27% | Source: arXiv Computer Vision
Lennart Schiweck, Alaa Saleh, Crist\'obal Curio
arXiv:2611.32548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligning inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals with text enables zero-shot activity recognition across wearable devices. A worn device's signal depends on its setup, the combination of body site and mounting. Leading IMU-language models make their encoders invariant to the mounting, which also discards the device's orientation relative to the body, such as the direction of gravity that separates sitting, standing and lying. We introduce SetCon, which replaces full invariance with selective invariance. It estimates each device's mounting on its known body site from a few unlabeled windows and conditions its encoder on this estimate. Because the mounting stays nearly fixed while the device is worn, the moving body serves as a calibration target. Both calibration and representation learning are supervised by 3D human motion, since one movement can be simulated under many known sensor setups. At test time, a class is represented by its name or by an anchor, which averages the text embeddings of the name and of activity descriptions and needs no labeled window. A language model built on the frozen encoder also answers how and in what order a movement is performed. Trained only on IMU simulated from the same Nymeria motion capture as AnyMo, SetCon reaches 56.6% mean zero-shot accuracy on 13 real datasets with class names and 65.3% with anchors, against 41.8% and 46.7% for AnyMo.
